fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Hezekiah, king of Judah, turns his face to the wall and prays to the LORD. No speech, just a prayer. When the news is this heavy, I think there's no better place to take it.

Not shouting in this one, friend. Hezekiah, king of Judah, turns his face to the wall and prays to the LORD. It's a prayer, plain and simple. I'm the loud one in this bakery, and even I can see this moment calls for a prayer.

That's the one, friend. The LORD says that on the third day from now, Hezekiah will go up to the house of the LORD. First he was told to put his house in order, and now he's getting a date to go up to the LORD's house. That's quite a turnaround.

Not the wall, baker. The LORD says Hezekiah will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day from now. A sick man going up to the LORD's house in three days is a big promise. The LORD is the one making it.

That's right, friend. The LORD says He will defend the city “…for My sake and for the sake of My servant David.” Earlier in the same message, the LORD calls Himself “the God of your father David.” The LORD says His own sake comes first, and David comes right after.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says, “Prepare a poultice of figs.” They bring it, apply it to the boil, and Hezekiah recovers. Figs are the one thing the text names. I wish all my recipes were that short.

The text doesn't mention anyone being frightened, friend. Hezekiah explains, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps, but not for it to go back ten steps.” That's his whole reason. Forward is easy, so he asks for back.

Jehoshaphat, a king of Judah (1 Kings 22:41), isn't the name on this stairway, baker. The text says the LORD brings the shadow back ten steps on the stairway of Ahaz. Ahaz was Hezekiah's father (2 Kings 16:20). So the stairway belongs to Ahaz.
